clue.text: London-Leeds road led windingly about close to Watford's centre

parts.note: the M1 motorway runs from London to Leeds, with the 1 written as the letter I

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled letters are placed around the single letter
something that winds twists about, so these letters do not stay in their printed order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter of the next word is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of Watford

explanation.surface: Directions for a motorway journey that wanders round Watford town centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main motorway north from London; crosswords often write its 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: The middle of something is its central point, so the two words are straightforward synonyms as nouns.

clue.text: The start of my newspaper column was really sad

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of my
an op-ed is an opinion column printed opposite the editorial page

explanation.surface: A columnist confesses that their first piece was a depressing read.
explanation.definitionFit: To mope is to sulk listlessly, so someone who moped spent time in a gloomy, dejected state.

clue.text: Idiots get into Oxbridge thus?

parts.note: surface reading: a jibe that fools somehow win places at elite universities
setter's reading: the keys belonging to a university lecturer would literally open the college doors

explanation.surface: A sneer that dimwits still manage to win places at Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as DON KEYS: a don is an Oxford or Cambridge tutor, and his keys get you into the college.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a donkey is a common British way of saying they are stupid or foolish.

clue.text: Not hard to add line within left-hand side's comprehensive margin

parts.note: standard abbreviation for left

indicators.note: not tells us to go without something, so the following letter is struck out

parts.note: taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

indicators.note: within means inside, so one letter sits inside a word

parts.note: taken as written
L is a common abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Instructions for ruling a margin line on the left of a page.
explanation.walkthrough: Left-hand side reads as one phrase but splits into three words; Not hard applies to hand alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A landslide is an election won by a huge majority, an overwhelming winning margin.

clue.text: Period of dreadful flu left Paddy getting a heart bypass

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a bad state, so these letters are messed up

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

indicators.note: a bypass routes round the heart, so the middle letter is skipped

parts.note: standard abbreviation for left
a paddy is a fit of temper, as is a strop

explanation.surface: A bad bout of flu leaves a man named Paddy needing heart surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like an Irish name; here it is a temper tantrum, and STROP loses its central R. Strop is British slang for a sulk.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a full stop is the punctuation mark Americans call a period.

clue.text: Remove weapons from the Security Council?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: read as two words, a branch of the United Nations

explanation.surface: A call to strip the UN Security Council of its weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as UN ARM: the Security Council is one arm of the United Nations.
explanation.definitionFit: To unarm is an older form of disarm, taking away someone's arms or weaponry.

clue.text: One making light of sea battling between two opposing sides

indicators.note: between places the jumbled letters in the middle, flanked on each side

parts.note: left and right, the two opposite sides

indicators.note: things battling are thrown about in a struggle, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shrugging off a naval battle fought between two enemy fleets.
explanation.walkthrough: Making light of normally means treating as trivial; here it means producing light.
explanation.definitionFit: A laser is a device that emits an intense, narrow beam of light.

clue.text: High winds ripped a door's bottom half off

definitions.note: plural phrase for a singular noun: one storm of high winds

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom half of a word is its second half, and off says to drop it

parts.note: ripped and torn are synonyms
taken as written
taken as written before halving

explanation.surface: A storm tears away the lower half of a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a violent rotating windstorm, a column of extremely strong wind.

clue.text: On 500 pieces of paper, Magritte's subject is an unreal vision

parts.note: Magritte's famous painting shows a pipe captioned Ceci n'est pas une pipe
D is the Roman numeral for 500
a ream is a quantity of sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Magritte painting his subject on a stack of five hundred sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the painter's subject comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe dream is a fanciful hope or fantasy that will never be realised.

clue.text: The arbiter of what's new excitedly puts, say, 'Coldplay's number one'

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the number one letter of a word is its first

parts.note: first letter of Coldplay

explanation.surface: A music tastemaker gushes about a top Coldplay single.
explanation.walkthrough: What's New Pussycat? is a Tom Jones song, so the cat is the one asked what's new.
explanation.definitionFit: The song title asks a pussycat what is new, cheekily making the cat the judge of novelty.

clue.text: Writer with skull, oddly, going around in a cape

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

parts.note: taken as written

parts.note: letters 1, 3 and 5 of skull

explanation.surface: An author with a skull, behaving strangely, walking about in a cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: Cape looks like a garment to go with the skull; it is the headland.
explanation.definitionFit: A cape is a headland jutting into the sea, and a peninsula is land almost surrounded by water.

clue.text: Uncover stone with letters inscribed on it?

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
rest in peace, the letters carved on a gravestone

explanation.surface: Removing the covering from an inscribed stone tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: The it refers back to the stone, read as a tombstone.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip is to remove a covering, layer or clothing, laying something bare.

clue.text: Clothes, unwrapped, are removed from sideboards

indicators.note: removed from says one thing is taken out of the following word

parts.note: a dresser is a sideboard with shelves for crockery

indicators.note: unwrapping takes off the outer layer, so the first and last letters go and the centre stays

parts.note: the middle letter of are

explanation.surface: Garments, freshly unpacked, are taken out of the furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: Clothes reads as a noun but is the verb: she clothes the child.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress someone is to put clothing on them, so dresses and clothes are equivalent verbs.

clue.text: Me and the Royal Marines help woman who's legless

parts.note: taken as written
RM is the abbreviation for Royal Marines
aid and help are synonyms

explanation.surface: Me and some marines help a woman who is drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Legless is British slang for very drunk; here it is literal, as a mermaid has a tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A mermaid is a mythical sea creature with a woman's upper body and a fish's tail instead of legs.

clue.text: Japanese delicacy American and his second son brought west

indicators.note: west is the left of an across entry, so a letter is carried from the end round to the front

parts.note: US is short for American, as in US troops
taken as written
no letters of its own: it points to the second S in the string, which stands for son, as the letter to move

explanation.surface: An American man moves his younger son out west.
explanation.walkthrough: US and HIS give USHIS; the second S, standing for son, moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is a Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, a classic speciality of that cuisine.

clue.text: Office worker concealed a sob, having started late

indicators.note: starting late means missing the beginning, so the first letter is lost

parts.note: something concealed is kept secret
taken as written
to sob is to cry

explanation.definitionFit: A secretary handles correspondence and records in an office, a classic clerical job.

clue.text: Pot's cover hiding the last piece of Dover sole getting cooked

the last piece of a word is its final letter

parts.note: final letter of Dover
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Pot's cover suggests a lid, but cover is the wordplay and Pot alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A casserole is a deep cooking dish with a lid, a kind of pot for slow oven cooking.

clue.text: Start to struggle and clamber frantically?

definitions.text: Start to struggle and clamber frantically?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is taken

parts.note: first letter of struggle

indicators.note: frantic movement is wild and disordered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone begins to struggle and climbs up in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer as well as building it.
explanation.definitionFit: To scramble is to climb or move hastily and awkwardly, using hands and feet in a hurried struggle.

clue.text: Peter Fonda produced this straightforward list of requirements

parts.note: straightforward and easy are synonyms

explanation.surface: The actor Peter Fonda drew up a simple set of demands.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy Rider is the 1969 road film that Fonda produced, co-wrote and starred in.

clue.text: Fish sign up for chippy

parts.note: a carp is a freshwater fish
to enter a contest is to sign up for it

explanation.surface: Registering a fish for a fish-and-chip shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Chippy looks like the British fish-and-chip shop; it is also British slang for a woodworker.
explanation.definitionFit: Chippy is informal British slang for a joiner, a tradesman who chips and shapes wood.

clue.text: Extraction of broken molar vet left unfinished

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before trimming

explanation.walkthrough: Left unfinished applies to vet alone, giving VE to add to the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An extraction is the act of taking something out, which is exactly what a removal is.

clue.text: Well, millions take too much within this depraved city

clue.text: Rain disturbed idler catching some Zs

clue.text: Solomon's astride small horse after short dash together

clue.text: Be up and down, then ultimately yield, diminished
